problem.title: Sending a demo shouldn't cost you the track.
problem.lead: Two things break every remote review: the file leaves your hands, and everyone ends up in a different part of the song.

leak.label: Problem 01
leak.title: The file walks
leak.body: A WAV in an inbox is a WAV on somebody else's drive. Once it has been downloaded you no longer know who holds which version, and you cannot pull it back.
leak.answer: The track you send already carries your voice, and the link to it expires.

drift.label: Problem 02
drift.title: The room drifts
drift.body: One person pauses, another seeks, a third hears the drop four seconds late. By the end everyone is just asking each other where they are in the track.
drift.answer: One person presses play, and the whole room hears the same spot.

realtime.intro: This is the hardest part of the system, so it is written from the ground up: start with what an ordinary web page cannot do, then the connection that fixes it, the conventions that ride on that connection, the delivery model, and only at the end what was actually built here.

items.stomp: So why add STOMP on top?

problem.title: The problem with ordinary HTTP
problem.lead: The entire web we are used to runs on a single rule: the server answers only when asked. That rule is enough for almost every website — and it breaks the moment you want a shared listening room.

points.0: The mechanism is called request–response. The browser sends a request, the server returns a reply, and the exchange is over. The server has no way to start a conversation. It only speaks when spoken to.
points.1: Now picture seven people in one listening room. The owner hits play. The other six need to hear that same moment, at that moment. But their browsers have no idea anything happened — and the server is not allowed to volunteer it.
points.2: The familiar workaround is to keep asking: every few seconds, send a request saying “anything new?”. It works, and it costs twice over. Users are always a few seconds behind reality, which is enough for the sense of listening together to disappear. And the server collects a mountain of questions it has to answer with “nothing yet”.

have.tag: What the ordinary web gives you
have.title: A server that stays silent until asked
have.body: Finding out whether anything changed means going and asking. Ask rarely and news arrives late; ask often and you burn resources on empty answers. Neither option is good.

need.title: A server that speaks the moment something happens
need.body: The owner hits play and, within tens of milliseconds, the other six know. Nobody asked. This is precisely where ordinary HTTP stops, and the reason the rest of this section exists.

websocket.title: A WebSocket pipe
websocket.lead: WebSocket solves exactly that by dropping the ask-and-answer shape. Instead of opening and closing a connection per question, both sides open one connection and hold it open.

0.title: It starts with a handshake
0.body: The connection still begins as an ordinary web request, but it carries a proposal: let us switch to talking a different way. The server agrees, and from that moment the link no longer follows request–response rules.

1.title: Both directions, at the same time
1.body: Either end can send whenever it wants, without waiting for a turn and without being asked first. This is the core difference: for the first time, the server may speak first.

2.title: Held open
2.body: The connection does not close after each exchange. No repeated handshake, no re-establishing who you are for every single message — which is where most of the cost of request–response goes.

3.title: Far lighter per message
3.body: An ordinary web request drags hundreds of bytes of overhead along every time. On a connection that is already open, that overhead drops to a handful of bytes. For a steady trickle of messages like playback position, the difference is large.

websocket.closing: The result: instead of a few seconds of lag and resources spent on empty questions, events land in tens of milliseconds and only real news travels the wire.

stomp.title: So why add STOMP on top?
stomp.question: “We already have a two-way WebSocket connection — why bring in STOMP as well?”
stomp.answer: Because WebSocket gives you a pipe, not a language. It guarantees that what you send arrives, and takes no interest whatsoever in what it is. As far as it is concerned, every message is just a run of characters. The three jobs below are ones WebSocket does not do a single line of for you.

0.title: Telling one message apart from another
0.body: A message just arrived: is it a chat line, a seek command, or a notice that someone joined? WebSocket has no concept of that. You are forced to invent a convention of your own, write the sorting logic at both ends, and rely on everyone remembering to follow it.

1.title: Delivering to the right person or group
1.body: The server is holding hundreds of connections. To reach the six people in one particular room, you have to track who is in which room, filter, and clean up when someone drops off. All of that bookkeeping is yours.

2.title: Letting listeners choose what they care about
2.body: One person has the chat panel open, another has closed it. There is no standard way to say “send me this, not that”. Once again you would be defining a subscription mechanism from scratch.

analogy.tag: The shortest way to see it
analogy.title: WebSocket sits under STOMP exactly as TCP sits under HTTP
analogy.body: TCP only knows how to move bytes between machines; it is HTTP that defines what GET means, what POST means, what a 404 is. Nobody rewrites HTTP for each new project. The same applies here: WebSocket handles the transport, STOMP defines the meaning — naming channels, subscribing to them, sending, reporting errors. A ready-made set of conventions both ends already understand, instead of one you invent.

sample.caption: Those “conventions” are very concrete. A STOMP message is plain text: the first line says what kind of action this is, the next lines say which channel it is for and what the content is, then the content itself. Readable by eye, no tooling required.

pubsub.title: Publish and subscribe, instead of sending to each person
pubsub.lead: This is the idea that makes the whole thing simple: the sender does not send to recipients. The sender posts to a channel, and whoever cares subscribes to that channel.

radio.title: Exactly like a radio station
radio.body: The station does not need to know how many people have a radio on tonight, who they are, or where they live. It broadcasts on its frequency. Anyone who wants to listen tunes in. A thousand more listeners does not make the station do anything differently.

0.title: Shared channel — the room's business
0.body: For anything everyone in the room needs to know: someone joined, the track changed, a message arrived. The server posts once and the whole room receives it.

1.title: Private channel — one person's business
1.body: For anything that concerns exactly one person: your request to join was approved or refused, or an error for something you just did. The other five receive nothing.

pubsub.closing: The real gain is that the server is freed from the question of who to send to. It only has to pick the right channel. An eighth person walks in, a third one leaves, someone drops off and comes back — not one line of the business logic changes.

system.title: How our system works
system.lead: With all three layers in place, this is what actually happens whenever someone does something in a room. The diagram is the whole picture; what follows walks the same path one stage at a time.

flow.title: Six stages of one action
flow.lead: Take the room owner hitting play. This is what happens, in order.

0.title: Open the connection and say who you are
0.body: On entering a room, the browser opens a connection to the server and sends its sign-in details along with it. Until identity is confirmed the connection is open but useless — this is the first gate, and everything after it depends on the answer.

1.title: Ask to listen to the room's channels
1.body: The browser tells the server which room's channels it wants. The server does not simply believe it: rooms here are private, so it checks whether this person really is the owner, currently in the room, or waiting for approval. Anyone else is refused.

2.title: Send the action up, through a single door
2.body: When the owner hits play, the browser sends that action up. Every action must go through the business logic; there is no shortcut that lets anything be posted straight onto a shared channel. Without that rule anyone could fabricate a message and broadcast it into a room, and everyone there would believe it, because a fake looks exactly like the real thing.

3.title: Check the rate before spending any work
3.body: Before the business logic is touched, the system checks whether this person is sending too fast. Putting the check here rather than later is deliberate: a connection firing hundreds of actions a second has to be stopped before it can make the database perform hundreds of pointless lookups.

4.title: Run the logic and write the data
4.body: Change the track, recompute the playback position, save it to the database. Throughout this stage nothing has been announced to anyone.

5.title: Announce only once the write succeeded
5.body: Only after the data is safely stored is the event posted to the room's channel and delivered to the other six. The order matters: announce first and then fail to write, and everyone sees a state that never existed. Each event also carries the server's clock, so browsers use that as the shared reference instead of trusting their own.

channels.title: The channels in use
channels.lead: Six channels, split into the two groups from the model above.

0.c: People joining, leaving, being removed; capacity changes; the room opening or closing

1.c: New messages in the chat panel

2.c: Play, pause, seek, track changes, and comments pinned to a moment in the track

3.c: Approval or refusal of a join request; current state sent privately to someone who just arrived

4.c: The exchange two browsers use to set up a direct voice connection

5.c: An error for the specific action that person just took

outbox.title: The event queue — Kafka and the outbox
outbox.intro: Some work cannot be done while the user waits. This section starts there: why anything needs queueing, what Kafka solves, where Kafka alone still falls short, and how pairing it with one database table means no event is ever lost or invented.

items.waiting: Work the user cannot wait for
items.outbox: The outbox: record the intent to send

waiting.title: Some work cannot be done while the user waits
waiting.lead: One user action usually drags other work behind it. The problem is that the trailing work is sometimes thousands of times slower than the action itself.

0.title: The verification email on sign-up
0.body: Creating an account row takes milliseconds. Sending an email means opening a connection out to the internet, waiting for the other side to answer, and taking a few seconds over it is entirely normal.

1.title: Merging a voice tag into a track
1.body: The audio tool has to decode the whole track, mix the tag in, and encode it again. A long track takes minutes. There is no version of this where a browser waits it out.

waiting.closing: Doing this work while the user waits means they stare at a spinner for minutes. Worse: if the mail server is down, the sign-up fails too — even though the account was created perfectly well. A side job kills the main one. The way out is to answer the user immediately and hand the slow work to something else to finish later.

kafka.title: What Kafka is
kafka.lead: Kafka is where that work gets queued. But it does not behave like an ordinary queue, and that difference is exactly why it gets chosen.

notebook.title: Picture a notebook, not a mailbox
notebook.body: Empty a mailbox and the letters are gone. Kafka behaves like a notebook: each job is appended as a line at the end, in order, written to disk. A reader only records how far down the page it has got — the line itself stays. So a consumer that dies mid-way can restart and carry on from where it was, and adding a second reader later requires no change at all on the writing side.

0.title: Channels — one notebook per kind of work
0.body: Sending email and processing audio have nothing to do with each other, so they live in separate channels. A channel can also be split into parts so several readers work in parallel, with order still preserved inside each part.

1.title: Reader groups — sharing work and covering for each other
1.body: Several processes reading the same channel can form a group. Kafka hands each member its own share and guarantees that a given part is handled by exactly one of them. If a process dies, its share is reassigned to the survivors.

2.title: A book for broken jobs, so one bad item cannot block the rest
2.body: Some jobs fail however many times you retry — malformed content, for instance. Retrying forever leaves everything behind it stuck in line. Kafka lets those be moved to a separate channel for inspection later, while the main queue keeps moving.

kafka.closing: It looks like enough at this point: write the job to Kafka and answer the user right away. But there is a gap, and it is not in Kafka.

dualwrite.title: Kafka alone still falls short
dualwrite.lead: The trouble is that one action now has to touch two separate systems at once: write data to the database, and queue a job in Kafka.
dualwrite.setup: A database offers transactions: several writes are grouped so that either all of them stick or none do. But Kafka lives outside the database, so it cannot be part of that group. There are only two places to put the send, and both are wrong.

0.title: Send to Kafka before the transaction finishes
0.body: The job is in Kafka. And then the transaction hits an error and is rolled back entirely — the account was never created.
0.result: Result: a verification email for an account that does not exist. An event describing something that never happened.

1.title: Send to Kafka after the transaction completes
1.body: The data is safely stored. But between storing it and sending, the process is killed, the server restarts, or the network drops.
1.result: Result: the account exists but the email was never queued. The user waits for a code that is not coming.

dualwrite.closing: There is no third option. As long as the send sits outside the transaction, there is always a moment where the two systems disagree. The way out is not picking the less-wrong option — it is making the send stop being outside the transaction at all.

outbox.title: The outbox — record the intent to send, inside the same transaction
outbox.lead: The name comes from an out-tray: you do not carry the letter to the post office yourself, you put it in the tray, and the postal worker collects it.

idea.tag: The shortest way to see it
idea.title: Do not send. Just record that a send is needed — in that same database
idea.body: Instead of calling out to Kafka, the business logic writes one more row into a dedicated table, right beside the business data, in the same transaction. The row says what needs sending and to which channel. Because both are writes to the same database, they belong to one transaction: either both exist or neither does. The dilemma from the previous chapter disappears — not because it is handled more cleverly, but because it no longer exists.

relay.title: So who collects the post?
relay.lead: A background process runs on a timer, reads the waiting rows, and sends them to Kafka for real. Simple enough in outline, but there are three things it has to get right.

0.title: No two workers holding the same job
0.body: When taking work, the process locks exactly the rows it claims and skips any another worker is holding. That is what lets several run side by side without an email going out twice.

1.title: Abandoned work has to return to the queue
1.body: If a process dies right after claiming, those rows would be stuck forever. So a claim is only held for a limited time; once it expires without finishing, someone else may pick it up. And every pass takes expired work before new work — otherwise a steady stream of fresh jobs means the abandoned ones never get a turn.

2.title: Not waiting five seconds to start
2.body: The process scans the table on a cycle, but that is only the safety net. Normally, as soon as the transaction completes, the system nudges it to run immediately — so the delay is close to zero. If that nudge fails, the periodic scan still catches the row. One for speed, one for certainty.

system.title: How our system puts them together
system.lead: With both in place, this is the real path of an event. The diagram is the whole picture — note the two dashed frames, because the boundary between them is the part worth remembering.

flow.title: Six stages, following one sign-up
flow.lead: From the button press to the email landing in an inbox.

0.title: The user hits sign up
0.body: The system creates the account and, at the same time, composes the entire email — subject, text part, HTML part. Composing it here rather than in the consumer matters: this is the point at which the user's language is known.

1.title: Two writes in one transaction
1.body: The account goes into its own table, and the email just composed becomes one row in the queue table. Two writes, one transaction. Nothing has been sent anywhere yet.

2.title: The user gets their answer immediately
2.body: The transaction completes and the server responds that the account was created. Everything that follows happens out of sight; the user waits not one extra millisecond for it.

3.title: The background process claims the work and sends it to Kafka
3.body: It takes the waiting row, marks it in progress, and only then sends it to the matching channel. That order matters: sending before marking means the consumer could finish before the row is recorded, and the job would be done a second time.

4.title: The consumer reads it and does the real work
4.body: For email: read the content, check it is valid, hand it to the mail server — sending both a plain-text and an HTML version so any mail client can display it. For audio: run the merge tool, which may take minutes.

5.title: Retry what might work, set aside what never will
5.body: A flaky mail server gets retried, with a widening gap between attempts, giving up after about a minute. Failures where retrying is pointless — malformed content, say — go straight to the channel for broken jobs without a single retry, so they do not hold up everything behind them.

lanes.title: The two lanes running today
lanes.lead: Everything asynchronous in the system goes through exactly this mechanism, and there are two lanes.

0.title: Outgoing mail
0.body: Sign-up verification codes, password resets, and other notifications. The content is composed in advance, so the consumer only has to send it.

1.title: Audio processing
1.body: Merging voice tags into tracks. Because each track takes minutes, this lane is given far more time before it is considered stalled — without that, the system would assume the consumer had died and hand the track to another one, merging it twice.

system.closing: There is a price, and it is inherent rather than a bug: because the user already got a success response at stage three, a mail server that is properly down leaves them looking at “your verification code has been sent” while the email never arrives. That is what you trade away when you move work into the background.

redis.title: Short-lived state — Redis
redis.intro: Some data lives for tens of seconds and then has to vanish by itself, while being read and written on almost every call. This section starts there: why that data does not belong in the main database, what Redis is, and the jobs we actually use it for.

items.problem: The data the main database is wrong for
items.usage: The three jobs we use it for

problem.title: Some data has no business being in the main database
problem.lead: The main database writes to disk, keeps data forever, and answers complicated questions. Those three strengths are exactly the three things the data below has no use for — while its costs still have to be paid in full.

0.title: A rate counter
0.body: Knowing how many calls somebody made in the last minute means incrementing a counter and reading it back, on every single call. Put that counter in the main database and even a plain read turns into a disk write, purely for the counting.

1.title: State that expires by itself
1.body: The wait between two verification codes is sixty seconds. A login session lives fourteen days. After that there is nothing worth keeping. But somewhere permanent never forgets on its own: somebody has to write the cleanup, and every check is still a query.

2.title: A sequence that runs in one piece
2.body: Increment the counter, compare it against the limit, then allow or block. If another call slips in between those three steps, both see themselves under the limit and both get through. What is needed here is the whole chain behaving as a single step.

problem.closing: All three are short-lived, simply shaped, and needed fast. That is very nearly the definition of an in-memory key–value store.

what.title: What Redis is
what.lead: Redis is a data store that lives entirely in memory rather than on disk. No tables, no relationships, no queries — in exchange, every read and write takes less than a thousandth of a second.

board.title: Picture a whiteboard, not a filing cabinet
board.body: A filing cabinet keeps everything for years, has an index, and can be cross-referenced — but every trip to it costs something. A whiteboard is the opposite: each line is one name and one value, writing and wiping are instant, and a line can rub itself out when its time is up. Nobody files records on a whiteboard; nobody opens the filing cabinet just to count how many times somebody knocked.

0.title: Keys and values, nothing more
0.body: Each entry is a name and a value. The value can be a number, a piece of text, or a set of items. There are no tables to join and no query to filter with — to read something you have to know its name in advance. That poverty is precisely what buys the speed.

1.title: Every key can expire on its own
1.body: A key can be given a lifetime as it is written. When that runs out Redis deletes it. No cleanup process, no extra “expires at” column to compare against the clock on every read. Short-lived data disappearing by itself is built-in behaviour, not something to write.

2.title: Commands queue up, they do not overlap
2.body: Redis handles commands one at a time, so a group of commands sent together runs from start to finish with no other call able to land in the middle. That is what turns “increment, then check the limit” into a single step instead of two steps with a gap between them.

what.closing: The trade is that Redis cannot stand in for the main database: no complex queries, no relationships, and data in memory is not where anything that must not be lost belongs. So every piece of business data — accounts, tracks, listening rooms — stays exactly where it was. Redis holds only the short-lived part. And one thing worth saying plainly, because the name invites the opposite assumption: Redis is not a cache here — nowhere in the system reads from the main database and stashes a copy here for next time. It is the only home the data in the next section has, not a layer standing in front of anything.

usage.title: In this project Redis does exactly three jobs
usage.lead: No more than three. All of them are short-lived state, but each asks a different question — so each uses a different kind of key and a different technique.

0.title: Holding login sessions
0.body: In this system, “who is signed in right now” is a question only Redis can answer. Each live session is a key. When a session is refreshed the old one leaves a trace behind: if that retired token is ever presented again it was almost certainly stolen, so every session for that account is revoked rather than just refusing the one call. On sign-out, an access token that has not expired yet is written to a deny list for exactly as long as it had left.
0.holds: Live sessions, traces of refreshed ones, and access tokens that have been signed out.
0.life: Fourteen days; a signed-out token only until the moment it would have expired anyway.
0.how: All of one person's sessions are grouped into a set, so revoking every one of them is a single question rather than a scan of the whole store.

1.title: Counting how often calls arrive
1.body: Every call into the system passes one shared counter: five hundred per minute, counted per account when the caller is signed in and per network address when they are not. Counting per account is deliberate — count only by address and a whole building behind one internet connection shares a single budget. A few paths are far tighter: ten sign-in attempts a minute, and twenty voice previews a minute because each one is a paid call to an outside service.
1.holds: How many calls arrived inside a one-minute window, per account or per network address.
1.life: One minute, then the counter falls back to zero on its own.
1.how: Increment, set the lifetime if this is the first one, compare against the limit — all three as one step, returning the seconds to wait along with the answer.

2.title: Blocking anything repeated too fast
2.body: The question here is nothing like counting: not “how many in a minute” but “has it been long enough since last time”. Resending a verification code or asking for a password reset has to be sixty seconds apart. Five wrong passwords lock the account for fifteen minutes; twenty from the same network address lock that address for thirty. Guessing more than twenty room codes in fifteen minutes is blocked the same way.
2.holds: A slot that is already taken — the existence of the key is the whole answer.
2.life: Sixty seconds for a cooldown; fifteen to thirty minutes for a lock.
2.how: Create the key only if nobody else has. Creating it means enough time has passed; failing to means the time left on that key is the number of seconds to wait.

storage.title: File storage — an external store and expiring links
storage.lead: A track runs to two hundred megabytes, and no file in the system may be openable by just anyone. Those two facts together decide how every file is uploaded, read and deleted.

what.body: Files do not live in the database, they live in an external store. That store is sealed shut: there is no address that opens a file directly. To read one you have to ask for a temporary, signed address with an expiry on it.

points.0: The database keeps only the file's key, never an address. Moving to a different store, or a different region, changes not one row of data.
points.1: Permission gets checked at the moment the temporary address is issued — the only place that knows who is asking and whether they are allowed.

why.body: Because the obvious alternative — an open store with permanent addresses — throws away the only place a permission check can happen.

points.0: An open store means anyone holding an address can read it, and addresses leak every way there is: screenshots, browser history, somebody forwarding one to a friend.
points.1: Permanent addresses stored in the database mean moving to a different store requires rewriting all the old data.
points.2: The price is clear and was accepted: an issued temporary address works for whoever holds it and cannot be revoked. Every expiry policy exists purely to narrow the consequences of that.

when.body: Four kinds of file, none of them public.

points.0: The original track a user uploads, and the watermarked version of it.
points.1: The spoken clips used as an audio watermark.
points.2: Profile pictures. This one has a wrinkle: people who sign in with Google arrive with a Google-hosted picture address, so one field holds two completely different kinds of value and everywhere that touches it has to tell them apart.

how.body: How a file gets uploaded is chosen by its size and by whether the contents need inspecting. The rule: large files go straight from the browser to the store, files whose contents must be checked have to pass through the server.

points.0: The expiry on a temporary address is not one shared number but varies by context, because the real needs genuinely differ.
points.1: Deleting a file always happens after the database write has landed. The other order leaves the record intact and the file gone — properly broken; this way the worst case is a leftover file, which is harmless.
points.2: That is exactly where the litter comes from, and there is no cleanup job today. All three known sources cost only storage rather than corrupting anything — which is why the trade is acceptable — but storage only ever goes up.

storage.visualTitle: Three ways to upload, chosen by size and by what has to be checked

0.title: The browser uploads straight to the store
0.body: The server issues a temporary address and then stays out of it. The file never passes through, so it costs no request thread and no bandwidth. The price is that the server never sees the file and can only check it indirectly.

1.title: Streamed through the server
1.body: The format has to be checked, so it has to pass through. But it is read as a stream rather than loaded whole, so each upload does not hold five megabytes of server memory at once.

2.title: The server holds the whole file
2.body: Small, but still routed through the server, because before accepting it the real duration of the audio has to be measured — and measuring means having the actual contents in hand.

table.title: How long a temporary address lives — five different numbers, each for a reason

0.c: Two hundred megabytes over a slow connection needs about that long.

1.c: It only has to outlive a single page view.

2.a: A profile picture inside a listening room
2.c: The room is handed addresses once on entry, and the screen stays open far longer than fifteen minutes.

3.c: A session spent listening together runs longer than an ordinary page view.

4.a: Asking for a link to play one track
4.b: The caller chooses, one minute to one day
4.c: The needs really do differ, so there is a range — with a cap enforced at both ends.

errors.title: Reporting errors, in the reader's language
errors.lead: A business error has to travel from the deepest part of the system — where knowing what HTTP is would be a design failure — out to a response with the right status code and the right words in the language the reader is using. The only way that works is by splitting it into three separate things.

what.body: Every error carries a short code, and that code is the only thing the business layer needs to know. The other two are derived from it at the outermost layer.

points.0: The code is chosen by the business layer — it only says “this is a not-allowed error”, nothing about HTTP.
points.1: The status code is looked up from the kind of error, at the layer that does know what HTTP is.
points.2: The wording is looked up from the code, in whatever language the reader declared. One code produces two different sentences for two different people.

why.body: Because without the split, the business layer would have to know which status code matches which situation, and what language the caller reads. Both belong to the outermost layer, and pulling them inward makes the core depend on the protocol it happens to be serving — HTTP today, possibly something else tomorrow.

when.body: Every error shown to a user takes this path. But there are exactly two ways out, not one.

points.0: The ordinary request path returns a response carrying a status code.
points.1: The realtime path has no notion of a status code, so the error is sent back to the person who sent the message, on a channel of their own. Both paths share one table of codes and one set of wordings; only the destination differs.

how.body: Codes are banded by module, so the code alone tells you where an error came from. The language is captured by the very first layer in the chain even though nothing uses it until the very last — because any layer in between can throw an error that needs translating.

points.0: Every code carries a fallback English sentence. It rescues the experience when a translation is missing, but it is also what makes a forgotten dictionary fail completely silently: the response still succeeds, the logs stay clean, only the wording quietly reverts to English.
points.1: The interface translates a second time from the code, using the server's wording only as a fallback — because the interface still has to fill in values and phrase things differently per screen.
points.2: The consequence: adding a new error code means changing three places, not one. Forget the third and that error quietly appears in English inside an otherwise translated interface.

errors.visualTitle: The path of one error, from the deepest layer out to the reader

0.title: The business layer raises an error
0.body: With exactly one code attached. There is no notion of HTTP here and no notion of language — only “this is wrong, and here is its code”.

1.title: The outermost layer catches it
1.body: One single place catches everything that escapes, rather than each spot handling it its own way. That is what makes error responses identical in shape across the whole system.

2.title: Look up the status code
2.body: From the kind of error the business layer declared. This is where “not allowed” becomes a number the protocol understands.

3.title: Look up the wording for the language
3.body: Using the error code itself as the lookup key, with the language recorded by that very first layer. Nothing found, and it falls back to the English sentence.

4.title: Assemble one response
4.body: Code, wording, and a trace id so it can be found again later. Extra detail is attached when there is any — how many seconds until a retry is allowed, or which form field was invalid.

table.title: The kind of error decides the status code — this lookup is the entire seam between business logic and protocol

0.c: Wrong at the input, before business rules even come into it.

1.c: We do not know who you are, or the credential has expired.

2.c: We know who you are, and you are not allowed to do this.

3.c: The thing being asked about does not exist.

4.c: The current state does not allow it — somebody changed it just before you, for instance.

5.c: Over the limit; the response also carries how many seconds to wait.

6.c: Correctly formed, but a business rule says no.

7.c: The system broke, not the caller.

library.title: Moving a 200 MB file without choking the API server
library.subtitle: Direct upload with presigned URLs, and search that filters on more than a keyword.
library.problem: Routing the file through the API server means every upload holds a thread and a buffer, and then the same bytes have to travel again to storage. All the user sees is a progress bar that does not move.
library.approach: The backend never touches a byte. It signs a short-lived URL, the browser uploads straight to object storage, and only once that succeeds does the backend write metadata.
library.detail1: Type and size are checked client-side before a URL is requested — a bad file is rejected before any bandwidth is spent.
library.detail2: Progress comes from the XHR progress event, so the percentage is bytes genuinely delivered.
library.detail3: Metadata is written in one transaction after the upload succeeds; a half-finished upload leaves no orphan row.
library.detail4: Search runs directly on PostgreSQL: substring matching on the title, combined with status, format and duration filters in a single query.
library.decision: No resumable uploads. Chunking, per-part state and orphan cleanup are three things to maintain forever, in exchange for very little at the scale of a single demo file.

voiceTag.title: Why a tag at 100% still sounded tiny
voiceTag.subtitle: Measure loudness to EBU R128, match the tag to the song, then mix.
voiceTag.problem: A mastered track sits around -9 to -12 LUFS. A voice tag — synthesized, or recorded on whatever the user had — sits around -20 to -27. That 10 to 15 dB gap meant the volume slider ran out of travel long before the tag was audible: 100% only ever meant "unchanged", never "as loud as the song".
voiceTag.approach: Measure the integrated loudness of both sources, work out the gain that puts the tag a fixed headroom above the song, and only then mix. After that the user's percentage finally does what its label promises.
voiceTag.detail1: FFmpeg pipeline: measure LUFS on both → apply gain to the tag → build the looped tag track → mix down to a new file.
voiceTag.detail2: The gain is clamped between −12 dB and +18 dB. Past that the correction does more harm than good: lifting a very quiet tag only surfaces its noise floor.
voiceTag.detail3: Anything below −60 LUFS is treated as unmeasurable rather than believed — near-silence reports a number that would ask for an absurd boost.
voiceTag.detail4: Synthesized and user-recorded voices share one path once they are WAV files; only the source step differs.
voiceTag.decision: Rendered server-side rather than assembled with the Web Audio API in the browser. The result has to be identical on every machine, and the final mix needs to exist as a file to be shareable.

liveRoom.title: Seven people, one track, the same second
liveRoom.subtitle: The server holds an anchor, not a stream. And nobody can listen in on anyone's signalling.
liveRoom.problem: Everyone is on a different connection with different latency, and anyone can reload mid-track. Pushing the playback position every second would be both expensive and still wrong.
liveRoom.approach: The server neither streams audio nor counts seconds. It holds an anchor: which track, at what position, as of when, playing or paused. Each client derives the live position from that anchor plus elapsed time.
liveRoom.detail1: No process ticks every second to write the position — state changes only when somebody presses a button.
liveRoom.detail2: One event carries the whole state; its type only tells a client whether the audio source needs reloading.
liveRoom.detail3: A sequence number on every event makes a late-arriving frame a harmless no-op instead of a jump backwards.
liveRoom.detail4: WebRTC signalling goes through a per-principal user queue rather than a shared topic — one member's SDP and ICE cannot be subscribed to by another.
liveRoom.decision: Ending a room pauses the music instead of clearing it, against the literal requirement. Undo has to restore the session whole — deleting the row would make music the one thing that did not come back.
